thread.title: After the Bell: Why the Dow’s 250-Point Drop Doesn’t Signal the End of the World - Barron's

author: Ben Levisohn and Teresa Rivas
title: After the Bell: Why the Dow’s 250-Point Drop Doesn’t Signal the End of the World - Barron's
text:
The Dow Jones Industrial Average tumbled 250 points as it gave away its early gains for the third day in a row. In today's After the Bell , we...
Illustration: Getty Images •...consider whether the market's wild things are here to stay;
•...why the latest departure at Chipotle Mexican Grill (CMG) might be good news;
•...and why tariffs against China might be bad news for tech.
The Volatile Market Is Here to Stay
Yesterday, stocks had two reasons to drop. Today, they had many, many more.
The S&P 500 fell 0.6%, to 2749.48, while dropped 248.91 points, or 1%, to 24,758.12. The Nasdaq Composite declined 0.2%, to 7496.81.
We can offer many reasons for today's decline: retail sales, which fell for a third straight month ; comments by Germany's Angela Merkel about the possibility of U.S. tariffs and a European response; and sliding Treasury yields . But maybe we should just chalk it up to higher volatility.
It's not just that the CBOE Volatility Index, or VIX, rose 5.4%, to 17.23, its highest since March 1. It's that after years of quiet trading, sizable moves are becoming common-place. Jim Strugger, derivatives strategist at MKM Partners, notes that the S&P 500's intraday range has averaged 1.3% so far this year, compared to an average of 0.86% over the five years beginning in 2013 and ending at the end of last year.
Five years is generally how long low-volatility periods last, Strugger says, so the recent volatility has arrived right on schedule. The scary part: The intraday spread was much higher during the high volatility periods in the 1990s and 2000s, averaging 1.7% and 1.9%, respectively. If anything, that shows that volatility could be set to get worse, not better, in the months ahead.
"Time will tell if the recent shock represents a transition into a high-volatility regime," says Strugger. "Though we've heard lots of hyperbole to describe this recent intraday volatility, if we're right about regime change, then even more violent swings should be expected going forward."
That doesn't mean stocks can't keep rising. But it does mean that we have to learn not to treat every 1% decline as the end of the world. — Ben Levisohn
Chipotle's Revolving Door
Uh-oh—another executive is leaving Chipotle Mexican Grill (CMG). But maybe it's not such a big problem after all, despite the fact the stock ended lower on Wednesday.
The burrito chain said that Chief Marketing Officer Mark Crumpacker, who has been with Chipotle since 2009, is leaving his post today. Given his tenure, Crumpacker helped steer the company through its numerous safety scares , as well as its push into digital.
Maxim Group's Stephen Anderson writes that the move shows that the company's new CEO, Brian Niccol, is wasting no time in making "his presence known," and that executive turnover isn't surprising, given that he took the helm earlier this month.
Anderson views this is as a good thing, as Niccol “checks all the boxes” in terms of what Chipotle needs—brand leadership, menu innovation, technology, and international franchise development, and he may lure some of his former colleagues from Yum! Brands (YUM) to join the Chipotle executive ranks.
Chipotle closed down 2.2%, at $319.66. — Teresa Rivas
Why Tariffs Matter for Tech
Tech was the best-performing sector in 2017 and a market leader again in 2018. Analysts have predicted more gains ahead —and even those who are cautious don’t see a tech bubble brewing, given the differences between today and 2000 .
Still, tech was having an off day Wednesday. While it may be easy to blame the government putting the kibosh on the Qualcomm (QCOM)- Broadcom (AVGO) deal, citing national security concerns, DataTrek’s Nicholas Colas argues that that argument feels hollow, given that other big names, like Apple (AAPL), Microsoft (MSFT), Facebook (FB), and Google parent Alphabet (GOOGL) also underperformed, despite being highly unlikely acquisition targets for foreign buyers, to say the least.
So what exactly is going on? Colas thinks that what’s really driving the selloff is the White House’s plans to seek tariffs on some $60 billion of Chinese goods, which has clear implications for tech.
That doesn’t mean it’s time to start selling all your shares of the Technology Select Sector SPDR ETF (XLK). Colas says we’ve seen this pattern play out before with the president: “Tough talk, followed by backroom negotiations, followed by more tough talk.” We’re just at the beginning of the process, so it’s hard to say how long it will take to play out—although we can certainly expect the administration won’t be shy about airing its feelings.
So while there may be more scary headlines ahead, capital markets will adapt, and the most recent news was probably just a convenient reason to sell tech, which looked ripe for a pullback.
In all, he believes that it will take some actual action, rather than bluster, to dent the bull case for tech. — T.R.
